## Paper

## Abstract

Pathogenic bacteria rely on the stringent response to adapt to hostile environments
encountered within the host. However, the mechanisms by which host-induced stress
activates this response remain poorly understood. Here, we identify iron-sulfur (Fe-S)
cluster damage as a conserved trigger of the stringent response in major Gram-negative
pathogens, including Salmonella enterica, Enterobacter cloacae, and Klebsiella
pneumoniae. We demonstrate that Fe-S cluster disruption—triggered by oxidative stress
or metal imbalance—limits intracellular pools of sulfur-containing and branched-chain
amino acids, thereby activating the (p)ppGpp synthetase RelA. We further show that
during Fe-S cluster stress, (p)ppGpp plays a dual role: enhancing bacterial fitness and
promoting virulence by upregulating the Salmonella SPI-2 type III secretion system.
These findings reveal a conserved mechanism by which pathogenic bacteria integrate
host-associated stresses into an adaptive transcriptional response that promotes fitness
and virulence, highlighting Fe-S cluster integrity as a central hub for environmental
sensing during infection.

---

## Introduction

To survive the hostile environments encountered within the host, bacterial pathogens
have evolved sophisticated strategies to sense and adapt to host-induced stresses (1).
One of the most conserved is the stringent response, which is mediated by the alarmone
guanosine tetra- or penta-phosphate, collectively known as (p)ppGpp. This second
messenger accumulates in response to nutrient starvation and transiently reprograms
bacterial physiology by modulating transcription, translation, and DNA replication (2–6).
Tight regulation of (p)ppGpp enables bacteria to balance growth and survival, positioning
the stringent response as a key adaptive strategy (7, 8). Consistently, mutants that fail to
properly regulate (p)ppGpp struggle to proliferate in host tissues and exhibit poor survival
during infection (3).

In γ-proteobacteria such as Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium (henceforth
Salmonella), (p)ppGpp levels are regulated by two enzymes: RelA, which synthesizes
(p)ppGpp in response to amino acid starvation, and SpoT, which both synthesizes and
degrades (p)ppGpp in response to various stress signals, including fatty acid and carbon
source starvation (9–12). An emerging body of evidence suggests that metal availability
also influences (p)ppGpp metabolism across several species, including Escherichia coli
(13), Salmonella enterica (14), Bacillus subtilis (15), Enterococcus faecalis (16),
Streptococcus pneumoniae (17), and Staphylococcus aureus (18). However, the
molecular mechanisms by which metal availability regulates the intracellular pool of
(p)ppGpp remain poorly understood.

Here, we demonstrate that disruption of iron–sulfur (Fe–S) clusters activates the stringent
response in clinically relevant γ-proteobacteria, including Salmonella enterica,
Enterobacter cloacae, and Klebsiella pneumoniae. We show that multiple environmental
stressors, such as oxidative stress and metal imbalance, promote (p)ppGpp accumulation
via the RelA protein by depleting branched-chain and sulfur-containing amino acids. This
response reprograms transcription to enhance stress adaptation and virulence, through
upregulation of the SPI-2 type III secretion system. Together, our findings establish a
mechanistic link between Fe–S cluster damage and (p)ppGpp signaling, uncovering how
bacterial pathogens sense and respond to environmental challenges during infection by
rewiring their physiology to promote virulence.

---

## Results

Manganese stress triggers (p)ppGpp accumulation by restricting the
pool of amino acids

Since the stringent response has been associated with metal homeostasis in numerous
bacterial species (13–18), we hypothesized that fluctuations in metal availability could
trigger (p)ppGpp accumulation. To test this, we first identified conditions where
Salmonella experiences metal stress, either through starvation or excess, using growth
as an indicator of metal-induced stress.

We initially induced metal starvation by growing Salmonella in MOPS lacking magnesium
(-Mg), iron (-Fe), zinc (-Zn), copper (-Cu), manganese (-Mn), or cobalt (-Co). Surprisingly,
only Mg depletion significantly reduced bacterial growth in our conditions (Fig. S1a-e).
Because trace metals could potentially support Salmonella growth, we used specific
chelators: DIP (Fe), TPEN (Zn), and BCS (Cu) (19–21). Each chelator impaired bacterial
growth, which was restored upon supplementation with the corresponding metal,
confirming effective metal limitation (Fig. S1b-d). For Mn and Co, we were unable to
identify any specific chelators for which the exogenous addition of the corresponding
metal could restore growth. Beyond starvation, we also assessed whether metal excess
(+Mg, +Fe, +Zn, +Cu, +Mn, +Co) was toxic to Salmonella. We found that excess Zn, Cu,
Mn and Co severely inhibited bacterial growth, while supplementation with elevated levels
of Mg or Fe (1 mM) did not affect growth under our experimental conditions (Fig. S1f).

Next, we monitored activation of the stringent response under the identified metal stress
conditions by measuring (p)ppGpp accumulation using thin-layer chromatography (TLC).
To prevent indirect effects of stress on (p)ppGpp accumulation due to reduced uptake of
radioactive ³²P, we first cultivated Salmonella with ³²P under non-stress conditions
(MOPS). This approach ensured efficient incorporation of the radiolabel into the
nucleotide pool, as evidenced by successful labeling of GTP (first lane in Fig. 1a). Then,
we diluted the radiolabeled Salmonella into stress-inducing conditions and monitored
variations in (p)ppGpp levels. Of the eight conditions tested, only the excess of Mn
triggered (p)ppGpp accumulation, independently of its associated counterion (Fig. 1a, Fig.
S1g).

To determine whether (p)ppGpp production was mediated by RelA or SpoT, we monitored
(p)ppGpp levels in a relA deletion mutant (ΔrelA) and in a strain containing a synthetase-
dead version of SpoT (spoT ) during Mn intoxication (22). While no difference was
E319Q
observed between the WT and the spoT mutant, the absence of RelA completely
E319Q
abolished (p)ppGpp accumulation in response to elevated levels of Mn (Fig. 1b). Since
RelA is primarily activated during amino acid starvation by uncharged tRNAs entering the
ribosomal A-site (23, 24), we tested whether the addition of tetracycline, an antibiotic that
blocks the entry of uncharged tRNAs into the A-site, could prevent RelA activation under
our conditions (Fig. 1c). In agreement with this hypothesis, tetracycline completely
abolished (p)ppGpp accumulation in the presence of elevated Mn levels (Fig. 1c-d).
Furthermore, supplementation with amino acids completely abolished (p)ppGpp
accumulation and rescued the associated growth defect of Mn-intoxicated cells (Fig. 1d-
e). Together, these results show that excess Mn triggers RelA-dependent (p)ppGpp
production by restricting the pool of amino acids.

Disruption of Fe-S clusters leads to (p)ppGpp accumulation in Mn-
intoxicated cells

Previous studies have suggested that Mn toxicity stems from its ability to outcompete Fe
for binding sites on proteins that cannot use Mn as a cofactor (25, 26). For instance, Mn
excess has been shown to interfere with heme synthesis, leading to depletion of
cytochrome oxidase activity and ultimately to the failure of aerobic respiration (25). To
determine whether Mn intoxication triggers the stringent response by disrupting bacterial
respiration, we measured (p)ppGpp levels after treating cells with potassium cyanide
(KCN), which inhibits cytochrome oxidase by binding to its iron center (27). Similar to Mn
excess, KCN treatment led to RelA-dependent (p)ppGpp accumulation (Fig. S2a), which
was fully abolished by the addition of tetracycline or amino acids (Fig. S2b). To test
whether this accumulation resulted specifically from cytochrome oxidase inhibition, we
examined a strain lacking all three terminal cytochrome oxidases (ΔcyoAΔcydBΔappB).
Although this strain exhibited a severe growth defect (Fig. S2c), we did not observe any
increase in (p)ppGpp levels in the absence of stress (Fig. S2d). Moreover, this strain
accumulated (p)ppGpp in the presence of KCN or excess Mn (Fig. S2d), indicating that
inhibition of cytochrome oxidases is not the trigger for (p)ppGpp accumulation under
these conditions.

Beyond heme synthesis, we reasoned that Mn might also directly interfere with Fe-S
cluster-containing proteins (Fig. 2a). To explore this hypothesis, we performed aconitase
assays, as aconitase activity depends on a functional Fe–S cluster (28). In agreement
with previous work (26), Mn excess led to reduced aconitase activity, supporting a
negative impact of Mn on Fe–S cluster-containing proteins (Fig. 2b). Interestingly, it has
been shown that disruption of Fe-S clusters causes multiple auxotrophies (29), a
phenotype we also observed under Mn intoxication (Fig. 1e). This effect can be explained,
at least in part, by the inactivation of the Fe-S-dependent enzymes dihydroxyacid
dehydratase (IlvD) and isopropylmalate dehydratase (LeuC), which are involved in the
biosynthesis of the branched-chain amino acids isoleucine, leucine, and valine (ILV) (24,
30–32) (Fig. 2a). In line with this model, we observed a rapid decrease in the pool of
branched-chain amino acids in Mn-intoxicated cells (Fig. 2c). However, supplementation
with ILV only partially rescued growth under Mn stress, suggesting additional
auxotrophies (Fig. 2d). Since Fe-S cluster biogenesis requires sulfur atoms from amino
acids (Fig. 2a), we wondered whether the addition of the sulfur-containing amino acids
cysteine (C) and methionine (M) could reduce Mn toxicity. In contrast with ILV
supplementation, we observed that addition of CM substantially rescued bacterial growth
in the presence of elevated Mn levels (Fig. 2d). These results suggest that sulfur-
containing amino acids mitigate Mn toxicity by promoting the regeneration of a functional
pool of Fe-S clusters. To test this hypothesis, we deleted hscA, which encodes a
chaperone involved in Fe-S cluster maturation (33, 34), and tested whether CM
supplementation could still rescue bacterial growth under Mn excess in this genetic
background. As expected, the growth defect of ΔhscA under Mn excess was not rescued
by supplementation with sulfur-containing amino acids (Fig. 2e), supporting that cysteine
and methionine mitigate Mn toxicity by supplying sulfur atoms required for Fe-S cluster
assembly. In addition, the hscA mutant also displayed a higher susceptibility than the WT
to Mn toxicity (Fig. S3a-b), leading to (p)ppGpp accumulation at lower doses (Fig. S3c),
which emphazise the importance of Fe-S assemblRy during Mn excess. Remarkably, the
combined supplementation of both branched-chain (ILV) and sulfur-containing (CM)
amino acids provided the most effective protection against Mn-induced growth inhibition
(Fig. 2d). These findings suggest that Mn-induced damage to Fe-S clusters results in
multiple auxotrophies: one arising from the loss of Fe-S-dependent enzymes required for
ILV biosynthesis, and another reflecting increased cellular demand for sulfur donors to
support Fe-S cluster synthesis.

Since reducing environments promote Fe-S cluster assembly and stability in vitro (35,
36), we hypothesized that the addition of the reducing agent thiourea might help bacteria
preserve a functional pool of Fe-S cluster-containing proteins, thereby limiting the
subsequent activation of RelA. Consistent with this hypothesis, we observed that addition
of thiourea abolished (p)ppGpp accumulation in Salmonella during Mn stress (Fig. 2f).
Interestingly, thiourea also prevented the elevation of (p)ppGpp levels in response to KCN
(Fig. S3d), which also interferes with Fe-S cluster-containing proteins due to its strong
binding to iron atoms (37). As a control, we confirmed that thiourea had no effect on
(p)ppGpp accumulation induced by serine hydroxamate (SHX), a serine analog that
triggers amino acid starvation by inhibiting seryl-tRNA synthetase (38) (Fig. 2f). In line
with these assays, thiourea specifically alleviated the growth defects associated with
excess Mn, supporting the functionality of Fe-S cluster-containing proteins under these
conditions (Fig. 2g, S3e). Likewise, another reducing agent — ascorbic acid — also
effectively suppressed Mn-induced growth defects (Fig. S3f). Thus, these data support
the role of Fe-S cluster status in regulating (p)ppGpp levels in Salmonella.

Next, we investigated if other clinically relevant Gram-negative pathogens could modulate
the stringent response in response to Fe-S cluster damage. To test this, we measured
(p)ppGpp levels in two other pathogenic γ-proteobacteria, Enterobacter cloacae and
Klebsiella pneumoniae, in the presence or absence of Mn excess. Similar to our findings
in Salmonella, we observed that Mn excess and SHX induced (p)ppGpp accumulation in
these species (Fig. 2h-i, S3g-h). Moreover, supplementation with thiourea completely
abolished (p)ppGpp accumulation during Mn stress, but not in the presence of SHX (Fig.
2h-i, S3g-h). Collectively, these results indicate that the regulation of the stringent
response by Fe-S cluster damage is not limited to Salmonella but is also conserved
across other clinically relevant pathogens.

Iron limitation promotes the stringent response upon conditions
inducing Fe-S cluster damage

Having identified that the disruption of Fe-S clusters homeostasis can elevate (p)ppGpp
levels, we wondered why iron starvation did not lead to (p)ppGpp accumulation under our
experimental conditions (Fig. 1a). One possibility is that pre-existing Fe–S clusters are
sufficient to sustain amino acid metabolism during iron starvation, thereby preventing
RelA activation. To test this hypothesis, we quantified branched-chain amino acids under
conditions of iron limitation and manganese excess. Although both conditions restricted
bacterial growth (Fig. S1b,f), the intracellular BCAA pool decreased only in Mn-intoxicated
cells and not in iron-starved bacteria (Fig. 3a). These data explain why bacteria fail to
stimulate RelA activity during iron starvation, in contrast to Mn excess.

Since iron is required for Fe–S cluster assembly, we reasoned that restricted iron
availability could influence the stringent response under conditions that destabilize Fe–S
clusters and necessitate their de novo biogenesis. To investigate this hypothesis, we first
identified a condition that induces a transient disruption of Fe-S clusters which allows
bacteria to resume growth after stress. We found that the addition of 0.5 mM Mn
significantly extends the lag phase of Salmonella but allows recovery, supporting that
bacteria successfully restored a functional pool of Fe-S clusters (Fig. 3b). Under these
conditions, (p)ppGpp levels rise rapidly in response to Mn excess and return to their pre-
stress levels within two hours (Fig. 3c, S4). In contrast, higher concentrations of Mn (1
mM) were bacteriostatic and led to the maintenance of elevated levels of (p)ppGpp over
time (Fig. 3b-c). Next, we determined how iron availability might affect the recovery of
Salmonella after mild Mn excess. To reduce iron availability in the medium, we used a
concentration of the Fe-chelator DIP that does not affect bacterial growth in the absence
of stress (Fig. 3d). Strikingly, limiting iron availability using DIP drastically increased the
lag phase following mild Mn excess and promoted the maintenance of the stringent
response, as observed at higher concentrations of Mn (Fig. 3d-e).

We next wondered whether iron limitation might also extend the stringent response under
infection-relevant stresses that destabilize Fe-S clusters. To explore this, we examined
the role of iron availability during oxidative stress, which destabilizes Fe-S clusters (39,
40) and elevates ppGpp levels via RelA by generating an amino acid starvation (41) (Fig.
S5a-d). In line with our model, iron limitation drastically delayed bacterial regrowth
following mild H₂O₂ stress and led to the maintenance of elevated levels of ppGpp over
time (Fig. 3f-g). Remarkably, both phenotypes were also observed during more severe
H₂O₂ stress (Fig. S5e-f). Given the similar response of Salmonella treated with Mn
excess or H₂O₂ , we examined whether Mn excess induces oxidative stress under our
experimental conditions. Using the PkatG_gfpOVA ROS-specific biosensor (42) in the WT
strain, we observed robust GFP accumulation following H₂O₂ treatment but no increase
after Mn exposure (Fig. S5g), indicating that Mn stress does not generate oxidative stress
in our experimental conditions.

To extend our findings to other pathogens, we performed the same approach for
Enterobacter cloacae and Klebsiella pneumoniae, both of which accumulating (p)ppGpp
in response to Fe-S cluster damage (Fig. 2h-i, S3g-h). As shown for Salmonella, we
observed that both species accumulate ppGpp – but not pppGpp – in response to H₂O₂
exposure and that limiting iron availability with DIP delayed bacterial recovery and
promoted the stringent response, as observed when H₂O₂ concentration was higher (Fig.
3h-i, S6a-b). Collectively, these findings demonstrate that (p)ppGpp levels are regulated
by iron availability, which governs the ability of bacteria to regenerate a functional pool of
Fe–S clusters following stress exposure, especially during oxidative stress.

Elevated (p)ppGpp levels reprogram bacterial transcription in response
to Fe-S cluster damage

Our previous data demonstrated that Fe–S cluster damage dynamically modulates
(p)ppGpp levels. However, whether activation of the stringent response contributes to
bacterial fitness under these conditions remained unclear. To address this, we first
compared WT and ΔrelA strains under Mn excess. High Mn concentrations exerted a
bacteriostatic effect on both strains (Fig. S7a). While WT and ΔrelA displayed similar
growth in the absence of stress, the ΔrelA mutant failed to grow at Mn concentrations that
still supported WT growth (Fig. 4a, S7b). Similarly, under oxidative stress, ΔrelA was
unable to grow at concentrations that allowed WT growth (Fig. 4a), supporting the idea
that (p)ppGpp contributes to bacterial fitness under conditions that damage Fe–S
clusters. We also tested the ability of both strains to produce an inducible GFP in the
presence or absence of stress. While GFP production was comparable between strains
in the absence of stress, both Mn excess and H₂O₂ completely abolished GFP synthesis
in ΔrelA but not in the WT strain, which sustained substantial GFP expression under
stress (Fig. 4b). Together, these results demonstrate that (p)ppGpp accumulation
enhances bacterial fitness following Fe–S cluster damage and allows the maintenance of
essential cellular functions such as transcription and translation.

Next, to elucidate how (p)ppGpp facilitates adaptation under Fe-S cluster damaging
conditions, we performed RNA-seq on WT and ΔrelA strains exposed to Mn excess. We
selected Mn over H₂O₂ to avoid confounding effects from ROS-specific genes (e.g., katG)
and used a mild Mn concentration (0.5 mM) that induces (p)ppGpp accumulation (Fig.
3b) while still permitting transcriptional activity in the ΔrelA mutant (Fig. S7c),
thereby minimizing transcriptomic artifacts. Under these conditions, the WT strain significantly
upregulated 255 coding sequences (CDS) and downregulated 55 CDS, whereas the
ΔrelA mutant only upregulated 33 CDS and downregulated 32 CDS (Fig. 4c-d, S7d-f;
Supplementary Data 1-4). As expected, both strains similarly upregulated mntP
(formerly yebN), which encodes the main bacterial Mn efflux pump and is under the control of the
MntR regulator (43) (Fig. 4e). This confirmed that both strains experienced Mn stress and
validated that our experimental conditions still allowed the ΔrelA strain to mount a
transcriptional response to environmental cues. Additionally, both strains upregulated the
iscR regulon (Fig. 4e), which governs Fe-S cluster biogenesis (33, 34) and is activated
under conditions that compromise Fe-S cluster integrity (44). Together, these data ruled
out the possibility that the increased Mn susceptibility of ΔrelA results from defective
expression of mntP or the iscR regulon.

Despite both strains upregulating mntP and the iscR regulon, the WT exhibited a broader
transcriptional response (Fig. 4c-d, S7d-f; Supplementary Data 1-4). Our analysis
revealed significant upregulation of genes involved in substrate transport, metabolism,
signal transduction, and stress responses (Fig. 4f). In accordance with previous work (45–
47), we also observed increased expression of the SPI-2 type III secretion system (SPI2
T3SS) apparatus (Fig. 4g-h), which is essential for intracellular survival within
macrophages and the establishment of systemic infection by Salmonella (48, 49). This
induction was exclusive to the WT strain and absent in the relA mutant (Fig. 4h),
suggesting that perturbation of Fe-S cluster homeostasis may serve as a (p)ppGpp-
mediated signal to promote SPI2 T3SS assembly during infection. In agreement with this
hypothesis, a similar trend was observed under mild H₂O₂ stress (Fig. S7g). Together,
these findings highlight how (p)ppGpp enhances bacterial fitness by reprogramming
transcription to support stress adaptation and virulence.

---

## Methods

Bacterial strains and plasmids
Oligonucleotides, strains, and plasmids used in this study are listed in Supplementary
Tables 1, 2, and 3. Additional construction details are provided in the Supplementary
Methods. E. coli EC100D pir-116 was used for cloning purposes with pTOX2 and grown
aerobically at 37°C in Luria–Bertani (LB) broth (Sigma) supplemented with 2% glucose.
Salmonella strains were grown aerobically at 37°C in either LB or MOPS minimal medium
(40 mM MOPS buffer, 0.4 mM tricine, 0.4 mM K₂HPO₄, 10 µM FeSO₄•7H₂O, 9.5 mM
NH₄Cl, 276 µM K₂SO₄, 500 nM CaCl₂, 525 µM MgCl₂, 50 mM NaCl, 2.9 nM
(NH₄)₆Mo₇O₂₄•4H₂O, 400 nM H₃BO₃, 30 nM CoCl₂, 9.6 nM CuSO₄, 80.8 nM MnCl₂,
and 9.74 nM ZnSO₄; pH 7.2), supplemented with 0.2% glucose as the sole carbon source
(referred to as MOPS throughout the manuscript). When indicated, the medium was
supplemented with additional compounds at the following concentrations: amino acid (aa)
mixture (40 µg/ml of each aa), thiourea ( 100 mM), reduced glutathione (50 mM), ascorbic
acid (50 mM), serine hydroxamate (SHX, 0.4 mg/ml), MnSO₄ (0.5 or 1 mM), H₂O₂ (0.5,
1, or 2 mM), MgCl₂ (1 mM), FeSO₄ (1 mM), ZnSO₄ (1 mM), CuSO₄ (1 mM), CoCl₂ (1
mM), MnCl₂ (1 mM), N,N,N',N'-tetrakis(2-pyridylmethyl)ethylenediamine (TPEN,
200µM), bathocuproinedisulfonic acid disodium salt (BCS, 100 mM) and 2,2'-dipyridyl
(DIP, 0.1 mM or 1 mM). Electrocompetent cells were used for the transformation of E. coli
and Salmonella. Antibiotics were used at the following concentrations where appropriate:
ampicillin (100 µg/ml), kanamycin (50 µg/ml), and chloramphenicol (34 µg/ml).
Genomic mutations were construct with pTOX2 vectors as previously described (56).
Briefly, the E. coli donor strain was mixed with the Salmonella recipient strain at a 1:5 or
1:20 ratio in a total volume of 1 ml. Cells were centrifuged at 6,000 g for 2 minutes, and
the supernatant was discarded. The remaining 100 µl was plated on LB agar containing
0.3 mM diaminopimelic acid (DAP) and 2% glucose and incubated at 37°C for 4 hours.
Subsequently, cells were scraped and restreaked on LB plates containing 2% glucose
and chloramphenicol. Single Salmonella colonies were then restreaked on LB with 2%
rhamnose. Finally, chloramphenicol-sensitive (CamS) clones were screened by PCR.

Growth assays

experiments under anaerobic conditions is technically extremely challenging, as all
steps—including growth and labeling—would need to be carried out entirely within an
anaerobic chamber. Moreover, anaerobic conditions themselves have been reported
to modulate RelA activity through nitrate reductase NirD (PMID: 34323689), which
would complicate the interpretation of such experiments.
To address the reviewer’s concern and assess whether Mn²⁺ excess induces ROS
production, we instead used a well-established fluorescent ROS reporter, a pkatG-
GFP fusion (PMID: 24439899). In contrast to H₂O₂ treatment, Mn²⁺ exposure did not
induce reporter expression (lines 225–228, Fig. S5g).
Consistent with these results, our RNA-seq analysis revealed no induction of katG
expression under Mn stress (Table 4). Likewise, other canonical oxidative stress
markers, including ahpC, ahpF, and sodA (PMID: 26279566), were not upregulated
(Table 4).
In addition, Mn excess led to the accumulation of both ppGpp and pppGpp, whereas
oxidative stress selectively induced ppGpp. This distinction is likely linked to the
impact of ROS on the cellular GTP pool and is now discussed in the revised
manuscript (lines 320–330).

we examined the effect of Mn excess in an hpxF mutant lacking five ROS-detoxifying
enzymes (PMID: 19447905), which is highly sensitive to oxidative stress. As
expected, this mutant was hypersensitive to H₂O₂ (panels A–B below) but did not
exhibit increased sensitivity to Mn excess compared to the WT (panels C–D below).
Together, these data support the conclusion that Mn excess triggers (p)ppGpp
accumulation independently of ROS under our experimental conditions.

production of branch-chain amino acids should be backed up by direct
measurements of amino acid pools after treatment with the divalent cation.
We thank the reviewer for this helpful suggestion. As recommended, we quantified
branched-chain amino acid (BCAA) levels using a commercial BCAA assay kit

significantly reduced intracellular BCAA levels. These data have now been
incorporated into the main figure (Fig. 2b and 3a) and are discussed in the revised
manuscript (lines 137–138).

We thank the reviewer for this insightful question. Mn²⁺ and Fe²⁺ share similar ionic
radii, chemical properties, and coordination preferences, allowing Mn²⁺ to compete
for binding sites normally occupied by Fe²⁺ in metalloproteins (PMID: 34037759).
However, unlike Fe²⁺, Mn²⁺ cannot support the electron-transfer functions required for
the activity of redox-active Fe-containing proteins (PMID: 28928443; PMID:
22991063). As a result, Mn²⁺ substitution can selectively impair Fe–S cluster
function.
In contrast, other divalent cations such as Zn²⁺, Cu²⁺, or Co²⁺ do not share the
appropriate coordination chemistry to effectively replace Fe²⁺ in Fe–S cluster-
containing proteins. Consequently, these metals are less likely to disrupt Fe–S
cluster metabolism in a manner sufficient to trigger the stringent response.
To experimentally address this point, we tested whether thiourea could rescue the
growth defects induced by excess Zn²⁺, Cu²⁺, or Co²⁺. Consistent with the specific
ability of Mn²⁺ to interfere with Fe–S cluster function, thiourea failed to rescue the
growth defects caused by these other metals. These new results have been
incorporated into the revised manuscript and are presented in Figure S3e.

cluster activity would further strengthen our model. To explore this hypothesis, we
performed aconitase assays, as aconitase activity depends on a functional Fe–S
cluster. Previous work in E. coli has shown that Mn excess reduces the activity of
aconitase, a canonical Fe–S cluster-containing enzyme (PMID: 28928443).
Consistent with these findings, we observed that aconitase activity in Salmonella is
also significantly reduced upon Mn excess, supporting the conclusion that Mn
interferes with Fe–S cluster proteins.
Importantly, when considered together with the observed decrease in branched-chain
amino acid levels, these results provide strong evidence for impaired Fe–S protein
function during Mn intoxication. These new data have been incorporated into Figure
2b, and the main text has been revised accordingly (lines 127–130).

H2O2 activate ppGpp production in bacteria either are defective in [Fe-S] biogenesis
or in [Fe-S] repair.

role for Fe–S cluster biogenesis in modulating (p)ppGpp production. The new data

We thank the reviewer for this important and thoughtful comment. We agree that
extending the analysis beyond Mn excess to other physiologically relevant Fe-S
cluster–damaging conditions is essential to strengthen the generality of our model.
To directly address this concern, we examined the expression of SPI-2–associated
genes in WT and ΔrelA strains exposed to mild oxidative stress (0.5 mM H₂O₂), a
well-established condition that destabilizes Fe-S clusters. Using qRT–PCR, we found
that SPI-2 genes are significantly upregulated in the wild-type strain upon oxidative
stress, whereas this response is strongly impaired in the ΔrelA mutant. These results
demonstrate that SPI-2 activation in response to oxidative stress requires RelA-
dependent (p)ppGpp synthesis.
Importantly, these findings are consistent with our RNA-seq data obtained under Mn
excess and align with previous studies showing that (p)ppGpp positively regulates
SPI-2 gene expression. Together, these results indicate that the transcriptional
activation of SPI-2 is not specific to Mn intoxication but represents a broader
response mediated by the stringent response.
Collectively, these additional validation experiments support our conclusion that Fe-S
cluster destabilization—whether caused by metal imbalance or oxidative stress—
promotes SPI-2 gene expression through (p)ppGpp signaling. The new data have
been added to the supplementary information (new Fig. S7g), and the manuscript
has been revised accordingly to better integrate earlier work on the regulation of SPI-
2 by (p)ppGpp (lines 283–284).

We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. A key distinction between Mn
intoxication (as well as SHX treatment) and oxidative stress is that Mn excess
induces the accumulation of both ppGpp and pppGpp, whereas H₂O₂ exposure leads
predominantly to ppGpp accumulation, independently of the presence of DIP.
Several non-mutually exclusive mechanisms may contribute to this differential profile.
First, we considered the role of GppA, the enzyme responsible for the conversion of
pppGpp to ppGpp. To directly test whether enhanced GppA activity could account for
the absence of detectable pppGpp during oxidative stress, we constructed a ΔgppA
strain and monitored (p)ppGpp accumulation under the same conditions. As
expected, pppGpp levels were increased under Mn excess and SHX treatment in the
ΔgppA mutant compared with the WT. Notably, pppGpp accumulation was also
observed in the ΔgppA mutant during oxidative stress, but not in the WT. However,
substantial levels of ppGpp were still detected in the ΔgppA mutant under H O
2 2
stress, indicating that enhanced GppA-mediated conversion alone does not fully
account for the observed ppGpp/pppGpp profile.
A second contributing factor likely involves stress-induced changes in the intracellular
balance of GDP and GTP, which serve as substrates for ppGpp and pppGpp
synthesis, respectively. Oxidative stress has been shown to perturb nucleotide pools
and, similar to what has been described during nitrosative stress—another Fe-S
cluster–destabilizing condition—may preferentially limit GTP availability, thereby
favoring ppGpp over pppGpp synthesis (PMID: 29487237). Such an imbalance would
bias alarmone production toward ppGpp, even in the absence of enhanced pppGpp
hydrolysis.
Together, these data indicate that the lack of pppGpp accumulation during oxidative
stress likely arises from a combination of increased pppGpp turnover and stress-
dependent alterations in nucleotide pool availability. As suggested by the reviewer,
we have now included a dedicated paragraph discussing this point in the revised
Discussion (lines 320–330).
